title: Railway & Train Set
strapline: Build the track, close the loop, and drive a journey that visits every child's station.
intent: Children solve a genuine spatial puzzle — curves, straights, bridges and junctions only work when they fit and the loop finally closes.
Children soak up positional and journey language — through the tunnel, over the bridge, next stop, all change — as they drive.
Children sequence a journey: first station, next station, last station, and predict what comes before they arrive.
Children share a resource that truly must be shared — one track, favourite engines, a single busy junction.
Children link the play to real railways in their own lives — the tube with Grandad, the station down the road.
implementation: Let children wrestle the track before you help — a loop that won't close is the best puzzle in the room, so offer one curve, not the answer.
Commentate journeys with deliberate prepositions: 'through the tunnel, over the bridge, and slowly into the platform'.
Name the stations after the children and call the stops in a fixed order, asking what comes next before you get there.
Give the railway real jobs — coal to the power station, parcels to deliver, passengers to collect — so journeys have a point.
Turn the junction into a turn-taking teacher: a signal to switch, a 'wait here' sign, words for whose train goes first.
Add tickets, a departures board and station signs so mark-making is something the play genuinely needs.
Talk about children's real journeys — who came by bus today? — and rebuild them in track.
key_questions: The loop won't join up — which piece do you think will fix it?
What's the next station, and who is waiting there?
Two engines have met at the junction — who goes first, and how do we decide?
How many carriages can your engine pull before it's too heavy?
Where does this tunnel lead — what might your train see inside?

impact.text: Children fit curves, straights and junctions together to close the loop, turning and swapping pieces until the track joins up.
Children pour out positional language as they drive — through, over, under, between, next to the platform.
Children count carriages onto the engine and match one passenger to each seat before the train may leave.
Children take turns at the junction and share engines and track, settling disputes with signals and words first.
Children narrate the railway as they run it — delays, lost tickets, the mail that must get through — using words like platform, signal and junction.
Children talk about real trains in their own lives and rebuild those journeys in track.
Children call the stations in a fixed order and predict which stop comes next before the train arrives.
Children connect couplings and slot track pins with careful, controlled fingers.

enhancements: A ticket office with a hole punch, paper tickets, a money tin and a departures board children run themselves.
Station name-signs — including the children's real local station — and a simple picture timetable.
Boxes and tubes for engineering new tunnels and bridges the track must be threaded through.
Freight jobs: parcels, pom-pom 'coal' and a mail sack that must reach the last station by tidy-up.
A signal you can actually switch — red and green — to run the junction fairly.
Photos from a walk to the real station: the platform, the boards, the driver who waved.
A broken-loop photo card for children to diagnose — which piece is missing?

playing_exploring: Every new layout is an experiment — what happens if the bridge goes here and the junction there?
Children replay their own real journeys, folding memory into the play.
active_learning: The unclosed loop is a problem children refuse to abandon — they swap pieces until it joins.
Delivering the mail means completing the whole circuit, stop by stop.
creating_thinking: Children predict which piece will close the gap — curve or straight? — and test by trying.
Two drivers, one junction: children invent their own signal rules and hold each other to them.
